items.text: An unwanted influx of formation fluid (gas, oil or water) into the wellbore because the mud's pressure fell below the formation pressure. Caught early, it is circulated out. Missed, it can become a blowout.
An uncontrolled release of well fluids at surface after every barrier has failed.
A stack of large valves on the wellhead (annular and ram preventers) that can seal the well, even cutting through pipe with shear rams.
Fluid pumped down the drill string and back up the annulus. It carries cuttings, cools the bit and holds back formation pressure with its weight.
Mud weighted up enough that its hydrostatic pressure balances the formation, used to regain control after a kick.
Barium sulfate powder added to mud to make it heavier.
A roller-cone bit with three toothed cones that crush and gouge rock.
Polycrystalline Diamond Compact bit. Fixed cutters shear rock; today it drills most of the world's footage.
A bit with diamonds spread through its matrix, used in very hard rock. It exposes fresh diamonds as it wears.
A motor hanging in the derrick that turns the drill string from the top, replacing the old kelly and rotary table.
A square or hexagonal pipe that transmitted rotation from the rotary table to the drill string on older rigs.
A downhole motor driven by the mud flow, used to turn the bit and steer directional wells.
A downhole tool that stores energy and releases it as a sharp blow to free stuck pipe.
When the drill string can't be moved up, down or rotated. A costly and common drilling problem.
Recovering equipment lost or stuck in the well, using tools such as overshots and spears.
Mud flowing into the formation instead of returning to surface. It lowers the mud column and can lead to a kick.
Shooting holes through casing and cement into the reservoir with shaped explosive charges, so the well can produce.
An explosive with a metal-lined cavity that forms a high-velocity jet able to pierce steel and rock.
A cable used to lower tools (logging tools, perforating guns, plugs) into a well.
Tubing-Conveyed Perforating: guns run on the production tubing instead of wireline, allowing long intervals to be shot at once.
A beam pump. The nodding horse head drives a rod string that lifts oil from wells without enough pressure to flow.
The group of separators, heater-treaters and stock tanks that collect and treat a lease's production.
Captures gas that would otherwise vent from tanks, so it can be sold instead of flared.
A tall stack that burns gas that can't be captured, for safety.
Methods such as gas, chemical or thermal injection that recover oil beyond primary and waterflood production.
The share of production (or its value) paid to the mineral owner.
The rig manager in charge of the drilling crew and the rig itself.
A floorhand who makes and breaks pipe connections on the rig floor.
Works on the monkeyboard high in the derrick, racking pipe, and looks after the mud system.
The operator's representative on the rig, who makes the final call on the well.
A machine that makes up and breaks out pipe connections automatically.
Hydraulic wrenches that grip and turn pipe to the right torque.
A chain thrown around pipe and pulled to spin a connection quickly. Now mostly replaced by machines.
Hydrogen sulfide. A toxic, flammable gas found in 'sour' reservoirs. Deadly at a few hundred parts per million.
An ice-like solid of water and gas that forms at low temperature and high pressure and can plug pipelines.
Heavy hydrocarbons that drop out of crude as it cools and build up inside tubing and flowlines.
Mineral deposits (calcium carbonate, barium sulfate) that build up in wells and equipment.
Formation sand flowing with the oil, which erodes equipment.
A column of salt that rose through overlying rock. Oil often traps against its flanks.
The large pipe connecting a subsea well or pipeline to the platform or vessel above.
The steel lattice structure that holds a fixed offshore platform on the seabed.
Floating Production, Storage and Offloading vessel: a ship that processes and stores oil at sea.
Sending sound waves into the earth (with vibrators, thumpers or airguns) and recording the echoes to image the subsurface.
A truck-mounted vibrator that sweeps a range of frequencies into the ground as an onshore seismic source.
The marine seismic source: compressed-air guns that release bubbles of air to make sound pulses.
A sensor planted in the ground that records seismic waves.
A seismic imaging method that uses the complete recorded wavefield to build a detailed model of the subsurface.
Protecting steel from corrosion by making it the cathode of a cell, often with sacrificial anodes.
A wear-resistant alloy layer welded onto drill pipe tool joints.
Connecting to a pipeline or vessel while it stays in service, without shutting it down.
A worker's rotation on a rig, often two or three weeks on and the same off.
